title: Fuel Economy and Car Design in R
text:
This post uses R to examine how vehicle weight and transmission type relate to fuel economy in the mtcars dataset.
Data: mtcars, bundled with R’s datasets package. The data were extracted from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine and are distributed as part of R.

library(ggplot2)

title: Fuel Economy and Car Design in R
text:
Load and Prepare the Data
The dataset has one row per car model and includes fuel economy, engine, weight, and transmission variables. I turned row names into a regular column and converted the transmission code into readable labels.

cars <- mtcars
cars$model <- rownames(mtcars)
cars$transmission <- factor(cars$am, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Automatic", "Manual"))
cars$cylinders <- factor(cars$cyl)

head(cars[, c("model", "mpg", "wt", "hp", "cylinders", "transmission")])

                              model  mpg    wt  hp cylinders transmission
Mazda RX4                 Mazda RX4 21.0 2.620 110         6       Manual
Mazda RX4 Wag         Mazda RX4 Wag 21.0 2.875 110         6       Manual
Datsun 710               Datsun 710 22.8 2.320  93         4       Manual
Hornet 4 Drive       Hornet 4 Drive 21.4 3.215 110         6    Automatic
Hornet Sportabout Hornet Sportabout 18.7 3.440 175         8    Automatic
Valiant                     Valiant 18.1 3.460 105         6    Automatic


The dataset is small, so a grouped summary is useful before fitting a model.

aggregate(
  mpg ~ transmission,
  data = cars,
  FUN = function(x) round(c(mean = mean(x), median = median(x), min = min(x), max = max(x)), 2)
)

  transmission mpg.mean mpg.median mpg.min mpg.max
1    Automatic    17.15      17.30   10.40   24.40
2       Manual    24.39      22.80   15.00   33.90

title: Fuel Economy and Car Design in R
text:
Visualize Fuel Economy
Heavier cars tend to have lower miles per gallon. Manual cars in this dataset often appear among the lighter, more fuel-efficient cars.

ggplot(cars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = transmission, shape = cylinders)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
    y = "Miles per gallon",
    color = "Transmission",
    shape = "Cylinders",
    title = "Fuel economy by weight and transmission"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 1: Fuel economy decreases as vehicle weight increases in the mtcars dataset.

title: Fuel Economy and Car Design in R
text:
Fit a Linear Model
I fit a simple linear model to estimate fuel economy from weight and transmission type. This is not a causal model, but it helps quantify the pattern in the plot.

mpg_model <- lm(mpg ~ wt + transmission, data = cars)
summary(mpg_model)


Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + transmission, data = cars)

(Intercept)        37.32155    3.05464  12.218 5.84e-13 ***

transmissionManual -0.02362    1.54565  -0.015    0.988

The fitted values below compare a light and a heavy car under each transmission type.

new_cars <- expand.grid(
  wt = c(2.2, 3.8),
  transmission = levels(cars$transmission)
)
new_cars$predicted_mpg <- round(predict(mpg_model, newdata = new_cars), 1)

new_cars

   wt transmission predicted_mpg
1 2.2    Automatic          25.5
2 3.8    Automatic          17.0
3 2.2       Manual          25.5
4 3.8       Manual          17.0

title: Fuel Economy and Car Design in R
text:
What I Found
In this dataset, vehicle weight has a strong negative relationship with fuel economy. Manual cars have higher average MPG, but transmission is also mixed with other design features: many manual cars are lighter. After accounting for weight in a simple model, the estimated transmission difference is smaller than the raw grouped average suggests.

title: My First Weeks in MDS
text:
The First Week of Classes
The first week was fast-paced and more intensive than I expected. We began working with R, Python, statistics, command-line tools, and collaborative workflows. I was especially surprised by how quickly the courses moved from basic concepts to practical exercises. Although I already had experience in AI engineering, the program introduced me to a more systematic way of working with data and communicating analytical results.

title: My First Weeks in MDS
text:
Looking Ahead
I am currently adjusting to the workload and learning how to manage several short assignments at the same time. The pace can be challenging, but I am becoming more comfortable with it. Over the coming months, I hope to strengthen my foundations in statistics and machine learning while connecting them with my previous experience building AI agents. I also look forward to exploring Vancouver and getting to know my classmates better.

title: Classifying Iris Flowers with Python

Load and Inspect the Data

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
iris_df = iris.frame.rename(columns={"target": "species_id"})
iris_df["species"] = iris_df["species_id"].map(dict(enumerate(iris.target_names)))

title: Classifying Iris Flowers with Python
text:
Compare Measurements
Petal length and petal width are the clearest visual separation in this dataset. Setosa flowers are especially distinct, while versicolor and virginica overlap more.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

for species, group in iris_df.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(
        group["petal length (cm)"],
        group["petal width (cm)"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.8,
    )

ax.set_xlabel("Petal length (cm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Petal width (cm)")
ax.set_title("Iris petal measurements by species")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Petal length and petal width separate the three iris species.





I also summarized the average measurements by species. Petal measurements grow steadily from setosa to versicolor to virginica.

summary = (
    iris_df.groupby("species")
    .agg(
        mean_sepal_length=("sepal length (cm)", "mean"),
        mean_sepal_width=("sepal width (cm)", "mean"),
        mean_petal_length=("petal length (cm)", "mean"),
        mean_petal_width=("petal width (cm)", "mean"),
    )
    .round(2)
)

title: Classifying Iris Flowers with Python
text:
Fit a Simple Classifier
To check whether the visual separation is useful for prediction, I trained a logistic regression model. The model uses all four measurements and is evaluated on a held-out test set.

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    iris.data,
    iris.target,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=521,
    stratify=iris.target,
)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=200)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
predicted = model.predict(X_test)

accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, predicted)
print(f"Test accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}")

Test accuracy: 0.921


The confusion matrix shows which species were confused in the test set.

confusion = pd.DataFrame(
    confusion_matrix(y_test, predicted),
    index=[f"actual {name}" for name in iris.target_names],
    columns=[f"predicted {name}" for name in iris.target_names],
)

title: Classifying Iris Flowers with Python
text:
What I Found
The Iris dataset is small but very structured. Setosa is easy to separate because its petals are much shorter and narrower. Versicolor and virginica are closer together, but the logistic regression model still classifies the held-out examples accurately. This supports the visual pattern: petal dimensions carry most of the species signal.

I studied English as an undergraduate and later completed a master’s degree in Linguistics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. During my graduate studies, I became increasingly interested in natural language processing, machine learning, and software development.
Before coming to Vancouver, I worked as an AI Agent Engineer Intern at Covestro, where I developed agentic AI applications using LangGraph, AWS Bedrock, MCP, and retrieval-augmented generation. I also worked as an AI/ML Software Engineer Intern at BMW, focusing on AI-assisted automotive testing, CAN bus data processing, and workflow automation.
I am now studying in the Master of Data Science program at the University of British Columbia. I came to Vancouver to strengthen my technical foundation and prepare for a career in AI and software engineering.

title: About
text:
Why Data Science
My background in linguistics first introduced me to the challenge of turning human language into structured information that computers can process. As I explored NLP and large language models, I became more interested in building complete AI systems rather than studying language alone.
I chose the MDSCL program to develop stronger skills in statistics, programming, machine learning, and AI. I am particularly interested in building reliable AI agents that can retrieve information, use external tools, analyze data, and complete multi-step tasks. In the future, I hope to apply data science and AI engineering to practical problems in industry.

title: About
text:
Outside of Data Science
Outside of data science, I enjoy cooking Chinese and Japanese food. Some of my favorite dishes to make are gyudon, mapo tofu, Japanese curry, and tomato and egg stir-fry. I also enjoy exploring Vancouver, trying local restaurants, and discovering new neighborhoods.
I recently moved to Vancouver, so I am still learning about the city and building a new life here. I especially enjoy its mild climate, diverse food, and proximity to both the ocean and the mountains.
